title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
event_hint: Empirical study on SWE-QA comparing semantic (vector-index) search against deep agentic search (grep-by-subagent) for repository-level code QA, finding retrieval both more accurate and cheaper.
problem: Code agents spend much of their effort locating code. The increasingly preferred design, deep agentic search, delegates exploration to an isolated subagent to protect the main agent from context pollution (context rot), but there has been little evidence on whether it actually produces better answers, and at what cost.
mechanism: Two architectures are compared head-to-head on a shared benchmark: a ReAct agent using a prebuilt vector index over the repository (semantic search), and a Deep Agent in which a planning orchestrator delegates exploration to an isolated subagent that returns only a condensed result (deep agentic search). Every failed run is then coded into a six-mechanism, five-symptom failure taxonomy derived from execution traces.

evidence.claim: Pooled over four language models on SWE-QA, semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly versus 46.2% for deep agentic search.

Semantic search produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of deep agentic search; Table 3 mean cost per pass for Gemini 2.5 Flash is $0.213 (semantic) vs $0.436 (deep agentic), and for Gemini 2.5 Pro $1.048 vs $1.526.
evidence.value: < half the cost per correct answer

evidence.claim: The single largest share of deep agentic failures, 41.8%, occurred at the planner-to-subagent hand-off (coordination breakdown), a failure mode impossible for the flat semantic agent; the architecture-failure association is very strong (chi-square 508.8 on 5 d.f., Cramer's V 0.56).

The within-model Pass-rate advantage for semantic ranged from 5.6 percentage points (Gemini 2.5 Flash) to 49.6 (Gemini 3 Flash), with 10.0 (Gemini 2.5 Pro) and 10.6 (Qwen3-235B); all four McNemar and Wilcoxon tests remained significant after FDR correction.
Deep agentic hand-off failures were usually silent, ending in a fluent and confident answer that was wrong.

evaluation_context: SWE-QA benchmark (repository-level code QA); four LLMs: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B. ReAct agent via LangChain (vector index, restricted to repo-structure lookup, retrieval tool, file reader) vs Deep Agent via LangChain Deep Agents framework (planning, virtual filesystem, sub-agent delegation). Fresh conversation thread per question; only the target repository available. LLM judge validated against an independent human panel on 800 stratified answers (human-vs-judge Cohen's kappa 0.74; human panel Fleiss' kappa 0.81).
limitations: Scope is read-only repository-level code question answering (SWE-QA), not patch-writing/SWE-Bench-style tasks. The two architectures necessarily have different action spaces (tools differ), which the authors treat as intrinsic to the paradigms rather than a confound. Generalization is bounded by SWE-QA and the four models studied. Only the front evidence pack (abstract, intro, related work, design, master results Table 3, and failure taxonomy) was reviewed.
project_relevance: Directly relevant to agent-acceleration (read/grep/glob). It quantifies that the widely adopted hierarchical grep-by-subagent design can be both less accurate and more costly than prebuilt vector-index retrieval for read-only repository QA, and it surfaces a concrete correctness risk: silent hand-off failures where the agent returns a confident but wrong answer. This challenges the assumption that context-pollution protection is free.
source_notes: Pooled accuracy figures (65.2% / 46.2%) match the average of the four per-model Pass rates in Table 3.
Cost-per-pass numbers and per-model breakdowns are taken from Table 3 (PDF Page 15).
